3. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong Port, the importer through its C&F agent submitted bills of entry No. 147790 dated 9-11- 2010, 140406 dated 25-10-2010 and 147799 dated 9-11-2010 respectively to release the goods imported under the aforementioned letters of credit as per invoice value. But Customs Authority assessed the goods at the rate of US$ 3,150.00 per MT vide Nothi No. AP/Sec-1/10-11. Under compelling circumstances, the importer released the goods on protest as per assessment of the Customs Authority and thereafter filed three separate appeals before the respondent No.2, Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) against arbitrary assessment of the customs authority. Upon hearing the parties and perusing relevant papers/documents, Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT (Appeal) allowed the appeals and directed customs authority to assess the goods at invoice price by his order dated 15-12-2010. 

 6. Mr Mizanul Haque Chowdhury learned advocate appearing for the appellant in all the appeals submits that customs authority imposed inflated value ignoring invoice value without following provisions of Valuation Rules, 2000 framed under section 25 read with section 219 of the Customs Act but Tribunal without considering provisions of valuation Rules passed the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be set aside. He also submits that it is apparent from the bills of entry that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of pre-determined value by the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong, beyond the scope of law but Tribunal without considering this legal aspect erroneously passed the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be set aside. He next submits that Tribunal failed to consider that though Valuation Rules, 2000, mandates that assessing authority shall follow the rules sequentially but in the instant case customs authority in violation of said mandate assessed the goods arbitrarily and whimsically as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He again submits that Tribunal failed to consider that customs authority assessed the goods applying the method prescribed in rule 9 of the valuation Rules without applying rule 4 to 8 though Valuation Rules, 2000, mandates to determine value of the imported goods applying prescribed methods sequentially as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He further submits that the customs authority arbitrarily imposed inflated value without affording an opportunity of hearing to the importer-appellant to produce evidence in support of invoice value and thus provisions of Valuation Rules, 2000, as well as principles of natural justice are violated as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd and 22 other, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217; the case of Amirul Islam (Md) vs Commissioner of Customs, reported in 18 BLC 77; the case of Transcom Cables Limited vs The Commissioner of Customs, Customs House (Import), Chittagong, reported in 18 MLR 97 and an unreported judgment passed by this Division in Writ Petition No.1138 of 2000 (M/s Shah Dairy Products Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Customs and others). 

 7. On the other hand, Mr Pratikar Chakma learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.4 by filing additional evidence swearing affidavit submits that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of contemporary data base value which was affirmed by the Tribunal in accordance with law as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and order. He also submits that customs authority assessed the goods on the basis of contemporary data base value to stabilize market of the country regarding milk powder with a view to create level playing field for all the traders of same product as such Tribunal legally and justly passed the impugned judgment and order. He further submits that the appellant has not come with clean hands to seek redress before this court because the appellant after releasing the goods on the basis of assessment by the customs authority sold the product to end users/consumers with profit and thereafter filed appeal for furtherance of its profit but the end users/consumers are the ultimate losers as such the appeal should be dismissed. 

 9. Admittedly, customs authority assessed the goods ignoring invoice value declared by the importer. We have gone through the relevant bills of entry annexed in the paper book. It appears from the bills of entry that there is an endorsement in the bills of entry in the following manner: 

 মাননীয় কমিশনার মহোদয়ের আদেশ মোতাবেক Loaded Value US$ 3,150 per MT হিসাবে Adj. 1.3293 তে বি/ই শুল্কায়ন করা হলো (Bill of Entry No. C-147790 dated 9-11-2010) 

 10. This court time and again directed the customs authority to determine value of the imported goods after considering contemporary international market price by giving an opportunity to the importer to place evidence in support of declared/invoice value and not assess the goods attributing adjective such as commissioner value, loaded value, recorded value etc. which has no sanction of law. Section 25(2) of the customs Act provides that subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the price referred to in that sub-section in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with the rules made in this behalf. 

 11. Section 219 of the Act empowers National Board of Revenue to frame rules and accordingly National Board of Revenue vides SRO No. 57 framed Valuation Rules, 2000 providing methods to apply in deterring value of the imported goods. Valuation Rules, 2000, is a guideline for the assessing authority to follow strictly in determining value of the imported goods. Rule 3 of the valuation Rules mandates that methods prescribed in Valuation Rules shall be followed sequentially. In many of the cases, this court directed customs authority to follow the rules strictly in sequential manner which should be reflected in the relevant nothi of customs authority. The apex court of the land in line with earlier decisions directed customs authority to afford the importer an opportunity of hearing to place his case in support of invoice value. Relevant portion from the judgment passed by our Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd. and 22 others, reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217, is reproduced below: 

 "the learned Attorney-General sub-mitted that the fixation of normal value in every case of imports upon notifying the individual importer would be an impossible task and, as such, for the sake of convenience, the revenue authority has fixed the value of the imported merchandise at a prior date through the Circular dated 3-7-94 for making the same as the basis for assessment of the customs duties in disregard of the invoice value, but the above submission cannot be accepted because in fixing the citizen with the liability of payment of tax, the concerned authority is required by strict compliance of law authorizing it to fix a citizen with the liability of payment of tax and the plea of impossibility of fixation of the normal value of the imported merchandise in the case of each individual importer upon hearing him or that upon affording him an opportunity to place his case, if any, in support of the invoice value, cannot be accepted and the respondents, under the law, cannot be allowed to resort to the practice of pre-fixation of the value of the imported goods for assessment of customs duties in that the Government or any other agency authorized by the delegated legislation cannot act in a manner which is not authorized or provided in the law or by the law". 

 12. Submission made by the Deputy Attorney General that the ultimate losers are end users/consumers of the product merits consideration. It is true that a section of traders by taking recourse of unethical process such as under invoice, over invoice import goods for personal gain. It is also true that because of such unethical process the market becomes unstahilized and small traders face difficulty to compete in the market. Big traders with their large capital try to establish monopoly in the market by abolishing marginal traders which not only create imbalance in the economy of the country but also affect the end users/ consumers who are compelled to buy the essential product with a high price from a syndicate monopolizing market of a particular product/item. But sitting in this jurisdiction in dispensation 'of justice, we cannot go beyond law framed by the legislators as such this court time and again directed the customs authority to follow the Rules, in this particular case, Valuation Rules, 2000. We are aware of the volume of work in the customs house but inspite of that in a civilized society we have to follow the rules framed under the law as such the assessing authority is required to record notes in assessing the imported goods at least briefly in one or two lines which will reflect that the law and rules has been followed. Otherwise, it is difficult for the court to do justice in the context of socio-economic condition of the country.
